opus-5.5.text:
I think the first version of Tuixue shows that what matters most is solving a real pain point, not how polished or technically impressive the thing is.

When I started it, the motivation was very simple. Many Chinese students, including people around me, needed to get a U.S. visa, and checking appointment availability was painful. You had to log in again and again and refresh the page, and the information was scattered and opaque. So the first version was really crude. It basically fetched the earliest available appointment dates for different consulates and put them on one page. The frontend was ugly, the backend was a few scripts, and there were probably a lot of edge cases I didn't handle well.

But people started using it right away, and word spread quickly, because it saved them time and reduced anxiety. That taught me a few things.

First, the value comes from the problem, not the code. If the need is real and urgent, users will tolerate a rough interface. If the need isn't real, no amount of engineering will save it.

Second, ship early. If I had waited to build something perfect, with accounts, notifications, and nice charts, I might never have launched, or the moment might have passed. Getting a minimal version out let real usage tell me what to improve next, like adding history, trends, or alerts.

Third, information transparency itself can be a product. A lot of what Tuixue did was just take information that already existed and make it accessible and comparable. That turned out to be really valuable.

And finally, if you're solving your own problem or your friends' problem, you have a huge advantage, because you understand the pain deeply and you get feedback immediately. That's a pattern I've seen again and again, even in my later work on open-source tools: build something you yourself would want to use, get it out quickly, and let the users pull it forward.

r001.rationale: The response says Tuixue’s value came from addressing a real, urgent user pain point rather than technical polish or engineering, and explains that early users validated the demand.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first version of Tuixue was embarrassingly simple. It was basically a script that polled the US visa appointment website every few minutes, checked whether any earlier slots had opened up, and pushed a notification when something changed. No fancy frontend, no accounts, no design to speak of. I built it because I personally needed to reschedule my own visa appointment and I was tired of refreshing the page by hand.

And I think that's the first lesson: the product came out of a real, concrete pain that I had myself. I wasn't guessing what users wanted. I was the user. That made every decision obvious, because I just asked, "Would this have helped me last week?"

The second thing it showed me is that one thing done reliably beats ten things done poorly. People didn't care that the site looked rough. They cared that when a slot appeared in Shanghai or Guangzhou, they heard about it within minutes. If the crawler went down for an hour, I'd immediately get messages. That reliability was the whole product. Everything else was decoration.

The third lesson is about distribution. I never did marketing. It spread entirely through word of mouth in student group chats, because when something saves you three months of waiting, you tell your friends. So I learned that if the value is sharp enough, you don't need to push it. You just need to make it easy to share and keep it working.

And the last point, which I didn't fully appreciate until later, is that shipping the ugly version early gave me real data. I saw which consulates people cared about, what times of day slots appeared, how often the site changed its structure and broke my parser. None of that I could have planned from a whiteboard. So if I had to compress it into one sentence: solve a real problem you have, make the core thing bulletproof, ship it before you're proud of it, and let the users teach you the rest.

r001.rationale: The response says Tuixue began with a real problem the speaker personally had, rather than guessing what users wanted, and contrasts that user need with a basic script and no fancy frontend. This communicates that understanding demand mattered more than the technology.

astra-6.text: I think the first version of Tuixue shows that the most important thing is whether you’re solving a real problem for someone. Early on, it’s easy to focus on making the product look polished or adding more features. But the first question should be: does the core idea actually help people? Build enough to test that, listen to how people use it, and let what you learn guide the next version.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes solving a real user problem and learning from users, but it does not identify user demand as more important than technology.

You can spend a lot of time polishing features, but the real question is whether people understand what you’re offering and find a reason to use it. An early version helps you test that. Then you can learn from how people actually use it and decide what deserves more work.
